sections.Items of Business and Board Voting Recom:
The company reported a record-breaking fiscal year, with total revenue reaching an all-time high of $416.2 billion. Services revenue grew 14% year-over-year, surpassing $100 billion for the first time, while company gross margin came in at 46.9%, up 70 basis points from the prior year. Diluted earnings per share hit an all-time record of $7.46, and the company returned over $110 billion to shareholders. New products introduced during the year included updated iPhone, Apple Watch, AirPods, and Mac lineups, along with expanded artificial intelligence features under the Apple Intelligence platform and a broad software design refresh called Liquid Glass.

The company's executive pay structure remained unchanged, built around three components: base salary, annual cash incentives, and long-term equity awards. Performance-based stock units vest based on total shareholder return relative to S&P 500 companies over a three-year period, and annual cash incentives are capped with challenging targets tied to overall company performance. Shareholders gave the pay program a 92% approval rating at the most recent annual meeting. The company also engaged with holders of 70% of institutional shares during calendar year 2025 through a mix of pre- and post-meeting outreach, year-round investor meetings, and quarterly earnings calls.

At the upcoming annual meeting, shareholders will vote on five proposals. The board recommends voting in favor of electing all eight director nominees, ratifying Ernst & Young LLP as the independent auditor, approving executive compensation, and extending the Non-Employee Director Stock Plan from its current expiration of November 13, 2027 to February 23, 2036. The board recommends voting against a shareholder proposal requesting a China entanglement audit, arguing the company already discloses sufficient information about its international operations and that the proposal would inappropriately interfere with ordinary business decisions.
sections.Corporate Governance:
The company operates under a corporate governance structure built around accountability, principled decision-making, and performance monitoring. It uses a single class of shares, meaning every share carries one equal vote. All directors are elected annually for one-year terms, and a majority voting standard applies in uncontested director elections. The roles of Board Chair and CEO are kept separate to strengthen board-level accountability, and robust stock ownership guidelines apply to directors and executive officers. The board also maintains a year-round shareholder engagement program and ensures directors have meaningful access to senior management and other employees.

The board takes director oversight seriously through several ongoing practices. A time commitment policy requires the Nominating and Corporate Governance Committee to review each director's various responsibilities. All quarterly board and committee meetings include executive sessions held without management present. The board, its committees, and individual directors conduct regular performance self-evaluations, including one-on-one interviews led by independent members. Directors also receive continuing education on ethics, compliance, governance, and emerging topics relevant to the company.

Shareholders retain meaningful rights and protections under this framework. Any shareholder or group owning at least 10% of outstanding shares can call a special meeting. Up to 20 shareholders who have held at least 3% of outstanding shares continuously for three years may nominate candidates to the board through proxy access. The company also prohibits directors and executive officers from short selling, trading in derivatives, or entering other restricted transactions involving company securities, and bars those individuals from pledging company securities as well.
sections.Our Corporate Governance Framework:
The company operates under a governance framework built around clear accountability and decision-making structures. All shares carry equal voting rights, and every director is elected annually to a one-year term under a majority voting standard. The roles of Chair and CEO are kept separate to ensure independent oversight at the board level. Directors are subject to stock ownership guidelines, and their outside time commitments are reviewed regularly to ensure they can fulfill their responsibilities. The board also conducts continuing education on ethics, compliance, and governance, and holds executive sessions at every quarterly board and committee meeting with no management present.

Shareholders have meaningful rights and access built into the governance structure. Any shareholder or group owning at least 10% of outstanding shares can call a special meeting. Through proxy access, up to 20 shareholders who have owned at least 3% of shares continuously for three years may nominate candidates to the board. The company also runs a year-round shareholder engagement program, and the board maintains significant interaction with senior management and other employees.

The board takes internal oversight seriously through several ongoing practices. It regularly reviews both board and executive succession planning, and conducts performance self-evaluations at the board, committee, and individual director levels, including one-on-one interviews led by independent directors. Each member of the Audit and Finance Committee qualifies as an "audit committee financial expert" as defined under SEC rules. Directors, executive officers, and employees are prohibited from short sales, derivative transactions, and pledging of company securities.
sections.Role of the Board of Directors:
The board is responsible for overseeing the CEO and senior management to ensure the company operates ethically and in the long-term interest of shareholders. Directors are expected to take a proactive approach to this role, and the company holds itself to high standards of responsibility and ethics. A majority of board members are required to be independent under the company's own governance guidelines, and the board has confirmed that all members except the CEO meet the independence standards set by Nasdaq. The board has three standing committees — an Audit and Finance Committee, a People and Compensation Committee, and a Nominating and Corporate Governance Committee — and all committee members have been determined to meet applicable independence requirements under both Nasdaq and SEC rules.

The board keeps its leadership structure under regular review, with the goal of bringing a wide range of perspectives to oversight and decision-making. Currently, the roles of Chair and CEO are held by separate individuals, a structure the board believes best serves the company. This separation is intended to let the CEO focus on running the business day-to-day while the independent Chair drives accountability at the board level.

Each of the three standing committees operates under a written charter approved by the board, which is reviewed and assessed annually. These charters are publicly available on the company's investor relations website. The overall structure of the board and its committees is designed to support effective oversight of management and corporate governance.

sections.Board and Committee Structure:
The board is responsible for overseeing the CEO and senior management to ensure the company is run ethically and in the long-term interest of shareholders. All board members except the CEO are considered independent under Nasdaq rules. The board has separated the roles of Chair and CEO, a structure it believes best supports effective oversight and accountability — allowing the CEO to focus on running the company while the independent Chair keeps the board focused on governance.

The board operates through three standing committees, each with its own written charter that is reviewed annually. The Audit Committee, chaired by Ron Sugar and including three other members, met nine times in 2025 and is responsible for overseeing financial statements, internal controls, risk management, regulatory compliance, privacy and data security, and the relationship with the company's outside auditors. The People and Compensation Committee, chaired by Andrea Jung and including two other members, met five times in 2025 and handles executive pay, equity plans, and oversight of workforce-related strategies and practices.

The Nominating and Corporate Governance Committee, also chaired by Sue Wagner and including two members, met four times in 2025. Its main responsibilities include identifying and evaluating potential board members, recommending changes to the board's size and composition, overseeing corporate governance practices, and monitoring the company's approach to environmental and social matters. All committee members meet the independence standards set by both Nasdaq and the SEC.
sections.Board Oversight:
The board takes an active role in overseeing strategy and risk, supported by several committees with distinct responsibilities. The Audit Committee handles financial matters, cybersecurity, privacy, and compliance, and leads general risk oversight. The People and Compensation Committee oversees executive pay and workforce-related matters. A Nominating Committee handles governance and environmental and social issues. Management, led by the CEO, runs day-to-day operations and reports significant matters back to the board. An Enterprise Risk Management Program, backed by a Risk Oversight Committee that includes the Chief Financial Officer and General Counsel, works to identify and monitor operational, compliance, and reputational risks. Executive and board succession planning is treated as one of the board's most critical duties and appears on the agenda at every regularly scheduled board meeting.

On compensation, the People and Compensation Committee reviews each year whether pay programs might encourage unnecessary risk-taking. It concluded that current programs provide an effective mix of incentives focused on long-term shareholder value and do not encourage short-term risk at the expense of long-term results. Risk-mitigating features include performance goals tied to specific financial measures, payout caps, clawback provisions on cash and equity, and stock ownership requirements. On privacy and data security, the Audit Committee receives regular updates from management including the Head of Corporate Information Security. A management Privacy Steering Committee, chaired by the General Counsel and including senior leaders across engineering, services, and marketing, sets privacy standards and handles compliance issues. A similar Online Safety Steering Committee addresses user safety issues, including those affecting children.

The full board directly oversees artificial intelligence strategy and receives regular updates covering investments, partnerships, regulation, and risks, with the Audit Committee focusing specifically on privacy and regulatory dimensions of AI. The company has published Responsible AI principles to guide its development of AI tools and models. The board has also adopted a Human Rights Policy based on the United Nations Guiding Principles, covering customers, employees, and supply chain workers, with the General Counsel responsible for implementation and reporting. Environmental progress, climate goals, and supply chain conditions — including worker protections — are reviewed regularly by the board and reported publicly through annual progress reports.
sections.Board Meetings and Attendance:
The board held four meetings during 2025, and every director who served that year attended all of the board and committee meetings they were required to attend. All directors also attended the 2025 annual shareholder meeting, and the same attendance is expected at the upcoming annual meeting. Each year, the board conducts a formal self-evaluation to judge how well it, its committees, and individual members are performing. The Nominating Committee sets the overall framework for this review, and the independent board chair leads one-on-one interviews with each director to gather candid feedback. Topics covered include board and committee composition, how meetings are run, peer reviews among members, and oversight of executive succession planning. Results are shared with the full board anonymously, and each committee separately evaluates its own performance and reports back.

The company has a written policy governing transactions between the company and people closely connected to it — including directors, nominees, senior officers, and shareholders who own more than 5% of company stock, as well as their immediate family members. This policy applies when the value of a transaction exceeds, or is expected to exceed, $120,000 in a single fiscal year and the related party has some form of direct or indirect interest in that transaction. The Audit Committee is responsible for reviewing and deciding whether to approve or reject any such transactions.

When evaluating these related-party transactions, the Audit Committee considers several factors, including the nature and size of the related person's interest, the total dollar amount involved, whether the deal was made in the ordinary course of business, and whether the terms are at least as favorable as what could have been negotiated with an unrelated third party. Some categories of transactions are pre-approved under standing guidelines, and the Audit Committee chair has authority to approve certain transactions independently, with a summary later reported back to the full committee for review.
sections.Annual Board and Committee Self-Evaluati:
The board met four times during 2025, and every director who served that year attended all board and committee meetings they were required to attend. All directors also attended the 2025 annual shareholder meeting. Each year, the board conducts a formal self-evaluation to judge how well it, its committees, and individual members are performing, with the goal of improving how the board operates over time.

The evaluation process is designed by the Nominating Committee, and Dr. Levinson, the independent board chair, leads it by holding one-on-one conversations with each director. Those discussions cover topics such as board and committee composition, meeting quality, how the board functions, peer assessments of fellow members, and oversight of executive succession planning. Directors can also speak privately with the Chair of the Nominating Committee about Dr. Levinson's own performance. Key themes from the interviews are shared with the full board anonymously. Each committee separately conducts its own self-evaluation and reports findings to the board, including a review of whether the committee is following corporate governance guidelines and its own charter.

The board has a written policy requiring Audit Committee review of transactions between the company and insiders — including directors, nominees, executive officers, and shareholders owning more than 5% of company stock, as well as their immediate family members — when the transaction exceeds or is expected to exceed $120,000 in a single fiscal year. The Audit Committee decides whether to approve or reject such transactions, though certain categories are pre-approved under standing guidelines, and the committee chair has authority to approve transactions in specific circumstances. When reviewing a transaction, the committee considers factors including the related person's stake in the deal, the dollar amounts involved, whether the transaction occurred in the ordinary course of business, and whether the terms are at least as favorable as what could have been negotiated with an unrelated third party.
sections.Related Party Policy and Transactions:
The company has a formal written policy governing transactions between itself and insiders — including directors, director nominees, executive officers, and shareholders who own more than 5% of any class of its equity securities, as well as their immediate family members. This policy applies when a transaction exceeds, or is reasonably expected to exceed, $120,000 in a single fiscal year and the related party has a direct or indirect interest in it. The Audit Committee is responsible for reviewing and deciding whether to approve or ratify these transactions.

When evaluating a transaction under the policy, the Audit Committee considers several factors, including the nature and extent of the related person's interest, the approximate dollar value of the transaction, whether the transaction was undertaken in the ordinary course of business, and whether the terms offered to the related party are no less favorable than what could have been negotiated with an unrelated third party. Certain categories of transactions are pre-approved under standing guidelines established by the Audit Committee, and the Committee has also delegated authority to its Chair to approve or ratify transactions in certain circumstances. Any transactions handled through these streamlined processes are later summarized and reported back to the full Audit Committee for review.

On the governance side, the full Board met four times during 2025, and every director who served that year attended all applicable Board and committee meetings. The Board also conducts an annual self-evaluation led by the independent Board chair, Dr. Levinson, who holds one-on-one discussions with each director to assess the effectiveness of the Board and its committees. Individual committee self-evaluations are conducted separately and reported to the full Board, with findings presented anonymously to encourage candid feedback.
sections.Business Conduct Policy:
Apple's code of ethics, called "Business Conduct: The way we do business," applies to all employees, executive officers, and directors, and covers principles including honesty, respect, and legal compliance. Suppliers, contractors, and other business partners are also expected to follow these principles when working with the company. Employees must complete training on the code when they join and every year after that. The code is reviewed and updated regularly with input from senior leadership to keep the guidance clear and current.

The company also maintains an insider trading policy that covers directors, officers, employees, and other designated individuals, governing how they may buy, sell, or otherwise handle company securities. Apple also follows set procedures for repurchasing its own securities. The company believes these policies are designed to support compliance with applicable trading laws and listing standards. A copy of the insider trading policy was filed as Exhibit 19.1 to the Annual Report on Form 10-K for the fiscal year ended September 28, 2024.

On related-party matters, several board members and executives serve in roles at other organizations that have commercial or charitable ties to Apple, but the company does not believe any director had a material personal interest in those relationships during 2025. One notable disclosure is that a family member of the former Chief Operating Officer is employed by Apple and received total compensation exceeding a reportable threshold during fiscal year 2025 through the filing date. That compensation was set according to the same practices applied to other employees with similar qualifications and responsibilities.

sections.Compensation of Directors:
The board is made up of directors chosen for a wide range of expertise, including senior leadership, financial oversight, technology, risk management, and global operations. Candidates are evaluated by the Nominating Committee based on their skills, backgrounds, and how well they fit the board's current and future needs. Over the past four years, three new members have joined and two long-serving members retired. The board also decided to waive its general guideline that directors may not stand for re-election after turning 75, specifically to allow Art Levinson, the Chair of the Board, and Ronald Sugar, the Chair of the Audit Committee, to run again, citing their deep experience, knowledge of the company, and the value of continuity in leadership roles.

Shareholders can recommend director candidates by writing to the company's Secretary at One Apple Park Way, MS: 927-4GC, Cupertino, CA 95014. A shareholder or group of up to 20 shareholders owning at least 3% of outstanding shares continuously for at least three years may nominate candidates for up to 20% of board seats for inclusion in the proxy statement. The Nominating Committee evaluates shareholder-recommended candidates using the same criteria it applies to all other candidates, and it reviews each director's outside commitments annually to confirm no one is overextended. As of its November review, the committee found no director had time commitments that would prevent them from properly fulfilling their board duties.

The nominees put forward for election bring a specific mix of skills highlighted in a board skills matrix, covering areas such as corporate governance, risk management, financial expertise, innovation and technology, privacy and security, global business, and environmental leadership. Among the nominees are Art Levinson, 75, who has led Calico since 2013 and previously served as CEO and Chairman of Genentech; Tim Cook, 65, who has served as CEO since 2011 and joined the company in March 1998; and Wanda Austin, 71, a director since 2024 and retired President and CEO of The Aerospace Corporation. Each nominee was evaluated and recommended to the full board by the Nominating Committee.
